To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

racial/ethnic disparities in HIV are associated with stigma, that stigma can be reduced by strengthening economic and community empowerment, creating common ingroups, promoting contact with people with HIV, and enhancing social supports and adaptive coping, and that these strategies can reduce racial/ethnic disparities.
societal stigma related to racial/ethnic minorities contributes to racial/ethnic HIV-related disparities through its manifestation at the structural, individual, and intersectional levels.

societal stigma related to racial/ethnic minority groups is associated with racial disparities in HIV risk and outcomes through structural (e.g., segregation) and individual (e.g., stigmatization and internalized stigma) mechanisms, and interventions that strengthen resilience to societal stigma can reduce disparities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and structural conditions that contribute to racial/ethnic disparities in health and the ways in which people living with HIV can be empowered to overcome these conditions.
understanding the role of stigma in the production of racial/ethnic health inequities.
the social determinants of health and the role of stigma in shaping the health of racial/ethnic minorities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stigma is associated with HIV disparities and that interventions to promote resilience to stigma can reduce these disparities.
the stigma and HIV disparities model is a conceptual framework that provides a detailed understanding of the mechanisms by which societal stigma is associated with HIV-related disparities.
stigma plays an important role in racial/ ethnic HIV disparities, and that interventions that promote resilience to societal stigma may be a promising approach to addressing these disparities.

the Stigma and Resilience among People of African Descent (STRAND) study will be a longitudinal study of African-American and Latino MSM and transgender women in the United States.
the Stigma and Resilience Model can be used to guide the development of interventions that address the structural, interpersonal, and intrapersonal levels of stigma.
we need to address the structural, interpersonal, and intrapersonal manifestations of stigma to reduce disparities in the risk and burden of HIV.

stigma is a fundamental cause of HIV-related disparities and that a resilience agenda can help reduce disparities.
stigma reduction strategies should be implemented at multiple levels and in a culturally sensitive manner.
